headline: Pregnant inmate escapes from prison vehicle in New Mexico
author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news
Authorities are searching for a pregnant prisoner who escaped custody in Albuquerque while being taken back to prison after a medical appointment, the New Mexico Corrections Department said Thursday.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, was sentenced to six years in prison after pleading guilty to four vehicle theft charges going back to 2024, the Associated Press reported, citing court records.
She was being transported back to the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in the city of Grants after a prenatal appointment Wednesday when she escaped, the corrections department said.
Department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said Taylor, who is in her second trimester, was not restrained during the drive, the Albuquerque Journal reported.

She was being transported by three officers who stopped to get food from a Whataburger restaurant, when she unbuckled herself and drove away, Roembach told the outlet. The vehicle was found about an hour later, but Taylor was not inside.
New Mexico authorities said Taylor has ties to the Albuquerque area and Texas, and they urged people not to approach her while a multiagency search is underway.
Reporter covering Russia
Russian Orthodox patriarch calls on Christians to tame AI, warns of ‘Apocalypse’

The head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, has said that Russia has a “crucial task” in a fight to prevent artificial intelligence from gaining the upper hand “over human will and reason.”

With advanced AI, “the fulfillment of the prophecies of the Apocalypse seems closer than ever,” Kirill said Thursday at a religious conference. He cast Russia as a keeper of “a religious perspective on global processes” and an “alternative to the civilization of consumption,” echoing rhetoric of President Vladimir Putin, who has pursued a traditionalist, conservative society cast as an alternative to the decadent West.
Kirill said taming this “incredible new power” and preventing a scenario in which humans are relegated to the margins of existence “rests specifically upon Christians.”
Russia’s biggest bank, Sber, issued a report this week that said AI can replace at least 13 percent of jobs in Russia and force another 38 percent to adapt.

Pope Leo XIV has voiced similar concerns, making AI the focus of his first encyclical. Leo called AI a powerful achievement that needs oversight and must serve the common good, while warning it could hollow out the middle class, drive unemployment and concentrate wealth among a few.
Trump’s Thanksgiving message attacks adversaries, migrants and economic data
President Donald Trump issued an acerbic Thanksgiving message Thursday that criticized the Commerce Department, members of the Somali community and opponents of his ballroom project.

Writing on Truth Social, he baselessly accused the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis of deliberately publishing “fake Economic Numbers” before the midterms. He cited updated figures published Wednesday which showed third quarter GDP growth at 4.3 percent, revised up from 3.4 percent.
The BEA updates its figures on a prescheduled basis. GDP often has big revisions after its initial release, as statisticians gather more data.
He also targeted those who sought to bring America to “the Radical Far Left,” and other political opponents.
He said Somalis in Minnesota who did not receive government assistance were “wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay … the others should be thrown out.”
Nearly 90 percent of Somalis in Minnesota are citizens, and only 1 percent are in America illegally, a demographer told The Post in 2025.
Trump also defended the time he spent on White House renovations, saying he “took time out of my very busy schedule to fix … a primary symbol of our Country.”
Many Americans have told pollsters they don’t see the renovations as a priority.
Reporter and researcher covering culture and social affairs in Asia
South Korea is cracking down on AI cheating with metal detectors and body cameras
SEOUL — South Korea has launched a nationwide crackdown on AI-assisted cheating after the top scorer on this year’s national tax accountant exam confessed to using artificial intelligence.

Han Won-seok, 34, admitted in a YouTube video that he photographed exam questions with a miniature camera, sent them to an AI tool and checked the answers on his phone. Police on Thursday were seeking an arrest warrant for him on charges including obstruction of official duties, local media reported.

In a country where students spend years preparing for one make-or-break test, the scandal has raised fears that AI is undermining trust in the system. Days after Han’s video, authorities rushed out new anti-cheating rules for the Suneung, the university entrance exam often compared to the SAT.

On exam day, Nov. 19, three emergency alerts blared on phones nationwide — to reveal any hidden devices in exam rooms — as part of last-minute changes that drew criticism from students, parents, teachers and lawmakers. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday, apologizing for the confusion it caused for half a million test-takers.
President Lee Jae Myung has ordered a review of how state exams are run and launched a task force to investigate suspected AI-assisted cheating in Suneung and national qualification tests.

The government plans to introduce metal detectors, device checks and WiFi shutdowns for middle and high school exams, as well as proctor-worn body cameras for national certification exams. Up to $373,000 is being offered for tips on major exam fraud, local media reported.
You should have a sinking fund for holiday spending. Here’s how to start one.

While some Americans are looking for ways to spend less this festive season, going into debt is still a holiday tradition for many. Pressure to spend on gifts, activities and family travel can lead to blown budgets and borrowing that many come to regret when the new year arrives.

A sinking fund offers a solution that allows you to spend without worry. Sinking funds are dedicated pools of money built by investing small amounts over time. Rather than struggling to find thousands to cover your December expenses, you can save for them all year.

While it’s likely too late to adopt this approach for the 2026 season, starting now for next year will allow you enjoy a much merrier time. Just decide how much you want to spend on the holidays, divide that amount by 12, and put the required sum into a special savings account earmarked for celebration. If you want to spend $1,500 on Thanksgiving and Christmas, set aside $125 a month until those holidays are here.
This approach allows you to truly enjoy the fun of the festivities, without the financial stress that often comes with them.
White House reporter covering President Donald Trump and his political movement
Trump to visit site for new semiconductor factory in Arizona

President Donald Trump is doubling down on boosting America’s semiconductor industry, planning to visit a chip factory in Phoenix next week after working to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in recent days.

Trump will deliver remarks and attend a groundbreaking ceremony Dec. 4 for an expansion at the multibillion-dollar Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company facility, according to a White House official.

The White House has not said whether Huang will also attend. The briefly ousted CEO is scheduled to appear before Congress next week. Trump and Vice President JD Vance helped get Huang reinstated to his position by providing assurances to Nvidia’s board members that the government does not have evidence that he poses a national security risk.
Lawmakers from both parties have pledged to investigate Huang’s romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has sought to promote the semiconductor industry, seeing it as a key driver of economic growth in the United States. The White House sees the Arizona plant as key to increasing U.S. semiconductor production.
